ateret-zekenim/part-001.txt.1:א: Even though it is not [d'oraisa], etc. From this we learn that those who do not separate challah from their dough—even though it is only d'rabbanan—there is no zimun among them (Rashba).
ateret-zekenim/part-001.txt.1:ב: And one does not bless on him, etc. Even without zimun; and the same applies to three who are under a vow of benefit from each other; but if one of them was under a vow of benefit from the two, they combine—for although he is not fit to eat with them, they are fit to eat with him. And so Tosafot wrote in the first chapter of Eruvin.
ateret-zekenim/part-001.txt.3:_: But if a Kohen and a non-Kohen ate as one and the Kohen eats and is careful, etc.—this is the view of Mordechai at the beginning of "three who ate" in the name of Maharam; and so too in Hagahot Maimoniot chapter 5 of Berachot. But the Agur wrote in the name of Shibolei Leket that even so they combine for zimun, since if it happened to them at their meal with ordinary bread of Israel both can eat together; and the view of Shulchan Aruch is primary, end of his words.

baer-heitev/part-001.txt.1:_: At the end. So wrote Rambam chapter 1 of Berachot. And Raavad challenged him and said thus: He erred in this—for they only said there is no zimun upon them to say they have no significance of fixed eating since they eat a forbidden item; but an opening and closing blessing—why should they not bless, since he benefits, end of his words. And Taz wrote Raavad only disagrees regarding one who eats b'shogeg; but if he ate b'mezid he does not disagree and is exempt from blessing, etc. He wrote in responsum Be'er Eshek siman 109: but one who is not careful about stam yeinam—even Rambam admits he blesses, etc. Beit Yosef wrote the same regarding one who steals wheat and grinds and bakes—even though he acquired through change he does not bless neither at the beginning nor at the end, etc.; and Magen Avraham disagrees and ruled they bless on it, for birkat hamazon—for he acquired through change; and so one should instruct, for birkat hamazon is d'oraisa and we go stringently; and it is possible even one who stole bread blesses birkat hamazon, for when he ate it he already acquired through change—see Magen Avraham. And Baer Heitev before me wrote in the name of Magen Avraham that one who steals wheat and makes bread blesses even at the beginning, and he was not precise.
baer-heitev/part-001.txt.2:_: Danger. And the same applies to one who eats forbidden food b'shogeg—for a place of danger and b'shogeg are one law for them (Taz). See siman 204 seif 9. And see Lechem Ketanot siman 252.
baer-heitev/part-001.txt.3:_: They combine. Agudah wrote chapter 3 "they ate": one eats cheese and two eat meat—they combine, for the one eating cheese can eat with the others. And on Shabbat on which the 9th of Av falls (within it) one does not invite zimun together those eating meat and those careful from meat and eating cheese, since none of them can eat with his fellow, end of his words. And Hagahot Minhagim challenged on this—for behold they can eat bread together; and so Rashi on Semag wrote they can invite zimun together. And so is the view of Taz—see there. Magen Avraham wrote one could say he holds they need to be able to eat together that same bread his fellow eats—and here they cannot eat meat and cheese from one bread, for it is soiled with meat as written in Yoreh Deah siman 89; and so Rokeach siman 65—that they do not combine unless the one eating cheese can eat meat; and so Hagah Maimoni in the name of Maharash: two eat meat and one milk—the one eating milk blesses and discharges the second because he can eat with his fellow and not the reverse—it implies specifically milk; but if he eats hard cheese they do not combine, for the custom now is not to eat meat after cheese; and on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls (within it) even with milk they do not combine; and there is practical difference at a mitzvah meal; and so is the custom—see Magen Avraham. And Baer Heitev before me wrote on this: this matter has no end, etc.; and I do not know why—and see Yad Ephraim. (And see in Eliyah Rabbah who expanded on this, see there).

beer-hagolah/part-001.txt.2:_: Rabbenu Yerucham in the name of Ramah.
beer-hagolah/part-001.txt.3:א: Tur in the name of Rambam and other poskim from that in Arakhin 3.
beer-hagolah/part-001.txt.3:ב: Tur in the name of R' Yitzchak from that of Rashbam.
beer-hagolah/part-001.txt.4:_: Berachot 45 and as explained in Tosafot.

beur-hagra/part-001.txt.1:ב: And one does not, etc. As written in the first chapter of Demai: demai, etc.—they bless on it; but on other [forbidden foods] they do not bless; and as written in Mezamnin; and in Tosefta chapter 2 of Demai: one said to his fellow, give me this loaf and I will eat it; this wine and I will drink it—they do not give him, for one does not feed pure foods to an am ha'aretz. If he was under a vow from the loaf and they said give me and I will eat it—a watermelon and they pierced it and said give me and I will eat it; wine and it was uncovered and they said give me and I will drink it—they do not give, for one does not feed a person something forbidden to him. Similarly a Jew may not hand a limb from a live animal to a ben Noach, nor a cup of wine to a nazir—for one does not feed a person something forbidden to him; and on all of these one does not bless, one does not invite zimun, and one does not answer amen after them. And in the first chapter of Sanhedrin and in the last chapter of Bava Kamma: behold one who stole a se'ah, etc.—this one does not bless, etc.; and in the first chapter of tractate Challah in Yerushalmi it teaches: stolen matzah is forbidden to bless on it, etc.; and see Beit Yosef.
beur-hagra/part-001.txt.2:_: Seif 2—if, etc. For blasphemy is not applicable; and see siman 318.
beur-hagra/part-001.txt.3:א: Seif 3—three, etc. Tosafot 45a s.v. ate, etc.
beur-hagra/part-001.txt.3:ב: And the same, etc. Even though he can ask now, nevertheless he did not ask. Tosafot there—for otherwise why need it to say there; it teaches us: since, etc.
beur-hagra/part-001.txt.4:_: Seif 4—one does not, etc. See siman 484.

chatam-sofer/part-001.txt.1:_: In Magen Avraham s.k. 1—to eat with his fellow. It appears to me one should be precise: for in the Mishnah at the beginning of the chapter "three who ate," one who ate demai—they invite zimun upon him—it implies the other two bless upon this one who ate demai; and so by law how is it possible that one who eats demai b'issur blesses? If so, what is the ruling—perhaps he declared his property ownerless? In any case these three; nevertheless these two are careful not to eat demai in its strict sense and cannot eat with this man—similar to those careful from gentile bread; and it turns out they cannot bless, and now too how can they bless? And one could say that if he declared his property ownerless he is forbidden to be stringent upon himself not to eat demai, since Beit Shammai hold one does not feed the poor demai, and it is forbidden to act like Beit Shammai as is known—and now too since he did not declare his property ownerless it is like demai and one of these two blesses. And with this the difficulty of Tosafot there daf 47a s.v. and Rav Huna taught: Beit Shammai say one does not feed the poor demai—and Tosafot challenged Rosh Hashanah: Beit Shammai's reason comes to teach us—and it should read thus—and understand well.

eliyah-rabbah/part-001.txt.1:_: (1) (Levush) One who steals an item, etc. And Bach rules regarding one who steals or robs wheat and grinds and makes it into bread—he is obligated to bless at the beginning and end, for he acquired through change; but one who steals bread or baked matzah is forbidden to bless on it at the beginning, but at the end he may bless—and see Magen Avraham that for the law his conclusion too is thus.
eliyah-rabbah/part-001.txt.2:_: (2) In a place of danger, etc. The view of Taz that even not in a place of danger, if he is b'shogeg, one may rely on him since many poskim hold one blesses on forbidden foods—see Lechem Mishneh and Kenesset HaGedolah; I abbreviated.
eliyah-rabbah/part-001.txt.3:_: (3) (Levush) Behold these, etc. Malbushei Yom Tov wrote one should not learn from this to three who ate when two or one eat meat and the other or others eat cheese—as I heard people say—for zimun is only on bread, and behold they can eat bread together, each cutting for his eating from the loaf and so the other, until here his words. And one must say it deals with hard cheese—for if it is soft cheese it is permitted to eat meat after it as explained in Yoreh Deah siman 89, and then they combine according to everyone. But one may wonder at Malbushei Yom Tov who ties the essence of this law to hearsay—and I found in Agudah first chapter of Eruvin and chapter "three who ate" and end of Taanit and Semak siman 109, and Rokeach siman 334. Also what he challenges—that behold they can eat bread, etc.—is already written in Hagahot Minhagim in the laws of the Ninth of Av, thus: when two eat, one meat and one milk—the one eating milk blesses and discharges the other because he can eat with his fellow and not the reverse. Small gloss in Mordechai on Shabbat before the Ninth of Av: one eats meat and one eats milk—they do not invite zimun together because they cannot eat with each other—and to the author it is difficult: but behold they can eat bread together, until here his words. And in truth it is not proper even for a great difficulty to reject an explicit law among great poskim; and perhaps they had a broad explanation without strain; also Hagahot Minhagim never meant to reject the law but only raises a difficulty—and there is no doubt that if Malbushei Yom Tov had seen all the words of the great ones mentioned above his heart would not be filled to reject this law. Again Magen Avraham was printed and I saw he too agreed with Hagahot Minhagim because they cannot eat one bread as written in Yoreh Deah siman 89. Also he wrote on what was challenged in Birkat HaZevach beginning of Arakhin on Hagahot Maimoniot: behold they can eat meat after waiting the measure—his words; he was not precise—for if he waits six hours the food will digest; until here. And I wonder at him—for he himself wrote earlier that according to Hagahot Maimoniot if one eats hard cheese they do not combine; and I already wrote in siman 173 one need not wait after cheese except one hour, and it seems even for birkat hamazon one need not bless between them—see there and understand. But in any case it is not proper to reject the essence of the law because of the difficulty in Birkat HaZevach—I avoided all the poskim mentioned above, see there; and further it is reasonable that at that time they must be fit to eat with each other; and so it seems from the case of vows of benefit so no poskim should distinguish between his vow and time. And I saw in responsum Maharam of Rothenburg siman 300 on a question where they vowed benefit for one day there is no distinction at all; and from the Stam it implies even for one hour they do not combine—and for this reason too we do not say they combine since if it happened at their meal with bread of Israel, etc.; and it is not similar to the beginning of the next siman where we say if they bring something they can eat—for there it is as if they did not finish the meal, but here in any case this one eating cannot eat with the other; and Taz expanded on this and what appears to my humble opinion I wrote.
eliyah-rabbah/part-001.txt.4:_: (4) Who are under vows, etc. When two are under a vow from the third they certainly combine, since the third can eat with them.

eshel-avraham/part-001.txt.1:_: D'rabbanan. See Baer Heitev s.k. 1; see under responsum Be'er Eshek; and the inquirer there—the reason is that the decree of stam yeinam is later than the enactment of blessings in the days of Ezra, and he compares it to Megillat Taanit where we say his vow preceded our decree; but in responsum Beit Yehudah he refutes this proof and also challenged him on the essence of the law.

kaf-hachayyim/part-001.txt.1:_: (1) [Seif 1] One who ate a forbidden item, etc. And those who do not separate challah from their dough—even though it is only d'rabbanan—there is no zimun among them. Rashba in the name of Raavad. Beit Yosef. Taz ot 1.
kaf-hachayyim/part-001.txt.2:_: (2) There—one who ate a forbidden item, etc. It is implied in Beit Yosef that the same applies to one who steals wheat and grinds and bakes—even though he acquired through change he does not bless neither at beginning nor end; but Bach wrote that even if you say regarding one who eats a forbidden item itself such as tevel, nevelah, and treifah, and even a d'rabbanan prohibition one does not bless at all—nevertheless regarding one who steals or robs a grain of wheat and grinds and bakes and makes bread it is obvious he must bless at the end, for he owes him money and it is not even blasphemy since he owes him; and for the opening blessing too it is possible he should bless; but one who steals bread or baked matzah is forbidden to bless at the beginning since he did not acquire through change, but at the end he may bless—see there. And they brought this in Shulchan Gavoah ot 4; and so is the view of Magen Avraham at the beginning of the siman; and so Rabbi Akiva Eiger ot 1; and it seems since there is a dispute here regarding birkat hamazon which is d'oraisa, he should bless so as not to add to his sin, and he should have intent in the responsum before the blessing to give the money to the owners; but for the opening blessing he should not bless but contemplate the blessing in his heart. And if he acquired it through change and afterward others took it from him, one could say even Beit Yosef agrees they bless. Acharonim. And so if he acquired through despair even for baked bread and afterward others took it—according to law he blesses at beginning and end (R' Zalman ot 4).
kaf-hachayyim/part-001.txt.3:_: (3) There—one who ate a forbidden item, etc. See Taz s.k. 1 who ruled that one who eats forbidden food b'shogeg blesses afterward—see there; and they brought Rabbi Akiva Eiger ot 2 and wrote one may rely on him since many poskim hold one blesses on forbidden foods—see there. And so R' Zalman ot 1; however in responsum Olah Shemuel siman 3 he challenged Taz and wrote that even if he ate forbidden food b'shogeg he does not bless—see there. And so in responsum Katav Sofer siman 22 he expanded on this and concludes for the law that even one who eats b'shogeg does not bless—see there.
kaf-hachayyim/part-001.txt.4:_: (4) There—and one does not bless on him, etc. For birkat hamazon—and the same applies to all closing blessings—they are a mitzvah; and if they blessed them on the forbidden item it would be a mitzvah coming through eating forbidden food which is a transgression. Levush.

levushei-serad/part-001.txt.1:_: Shulchan Aruch seif 1—only d'rabbanan. See responsum Bach Chadashot siman 1.
levushei-serad/part-001.txt.2:_: Taz s.k. 1—these b'mezid, etc. Somewhat difficult—for in siman 199 it is proven they invite zimun on all who did not, etc. And perhaps his intent is since he eats before these two it is public and they do not invite zimun—see Magen Avraham siman 199 s.k. 2 that one can explain his words too thus: everything depends on publicity—see there. And see Yoreh Deah at the beginning of the laws of slaughter how many constitute publicity—see there.
levushei-serad/part-001.txt.3:_: Magen Avraham s.k. 1—and what is written the same in chapter 6 of matzah—as it should read.
levushei-serad/part-001.txt.4:_: Taz s.k. 1—the words of Raavad and Rosh; nevertheless for the law—as it should read.

machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:א: As Magen Avraham wrote, as Rabbeinu Yosef wrote, etc.—that he acquired through change he does not bless, for it is blasphemy.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ב: And so responsum 649 that he wrote regarding a stolen lulav—even if he acquired through change without support of the mitzvah, even though he fulfills with it, nevertheless he does not bless on it.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ג: And so from the words of Rama siman 454 that he wrote: it turns out regarding stolen matzah one does not fulfill; but one who stole wheat and made it matzah and acquired through change—he fulfills. And Rama wrote: and regarding blessing see siman 649—it implies he holds as in siman 649 one does not bless—the same regarding matzah.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ד: And siman 11 regarding tzitzit stolen and acquired through change Rama also wrote and regarding blessing see siman 649. And further in siman 649 he is uncertain, etc.—meaning that which Shulchan Aruch wrote there that even if he acquired without support they do not bless—is explained in Rabbeinu Yosef there that he ruled thus because he is uncertain whether the essence of Tosafot's words that which we say stolen lulav—even on the second day of Yom Tov when we do not need "for you" one does not fulfill with it because it is a mitzvah coming through transgression—and they proved that if he acquired without support of the mitzvah—that is, before performing the mitzvah—there is no issue of mitzvah coming through transgression; and they challenged from that Abbaye said in Bava Kamma that R' Meir holds change does not acquire—from that R' Meir said: behold one who stole wheat and ground and baked and separated challah—this one does not bless but blasphemes; and how can it be change acquires—why is it called blasphemy? And Rava answered that R' Meir indeed holds change acquires, and that which is called blasphemy is because it is a mitzvah coming through transgression—behold even if he acquired through change before the mitzvah nevertheless it is mitzvah coming through transgression. And two answers: first answer—Rava's answer is only a rejection; but the truth is R' Meir holds change does not acquire; but if change acquires in such a case where he acquired through change it is not blasphemy. Second answer—blessing is different—for even though if he acquired through change for fulfilling the mitzvah it is not mitzvah coming through transgression, nevertheless it is not fit to bless on it and it is blasphemy; and if so in the first answer if he acquired through change it is not mitzvah coming through transgression even for blessing and he may bless; and in the second answer one does not bless; and since Rabbeinu Yosef was uncertain which answer is primary he wrote uncertainly that one does not bless; and if so we distinguish in other blessings but for birkat hamazon we hold in siman 484 that if he has doubt in birkat hamazon he must bless since it is d'oraisa.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ה: And what is written the same in chapter 6 of matzah, etc.—as it should read.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ו: (s.k. 1) One does not, etc. And on Shabbat on which 9th of Av falls—meaning a week in which 9th of Av falls, as Rabbeinu Yosef wrote in siman 551 seif 9—it depends on the custom: some refrain from eating meat in the week in which 9th of Av falls and some do not refrain.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ז: For behold Kohen and non-Kohen, etc.—for from this flows this law, since we say at the beginning of Eruvin: all are obligated in zimun—Kohanim, Levites, and Israelites. And we say: it is obvious; and it answers: it is not needed—for Kohanim eat terumah and a non-Kohen shares; lest you say since a non-Kohen cannot eat terumah he does not combine—it teaches us that since a Kohen can eat ordinary food it is fine; and it teaches us in any case that Kohen and non-Kohen can eat other bread.
machatzit-hashekel/part-001.txt.1:ח: As Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Agur—meaning the Agur also wrote like Hagahot Minhagim; and Rabbeinu Yosef rejected his words from the Gemara in Eruvin mentioned above.
